answer: The RBI requires commercial banks to ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and the Rules made thereunder. Furthermore, banks must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications on the matter issued from time to time by the RBI based on advice received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India. [S1]
According to [S1], paragraph 10(2), a commercial bank must review its money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually.

According to [S1], if an existing customer has not submitted the PAN, equivalent e-document, or Form No. 60 by the notified date, the bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the required documents. Before temporarily ceasing operations, the bank must give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

According to [S4], a commercial bank must monitor the 'at par' cheque facility and review the arrangements to assess credit risk and reputational risk arising therefrom. The bank also retains the right to verify records maintained by co-operative banks/societies for compliance with KYC and AML instructions under such arrangements.
[S1] specifies that for a remittance of ₹50,000 or more, a commercial bank must effect the transaction by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques, and not against cash payment.

According to [S1], a commercial bank should consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time and publicly available information for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations.
According to [S1], a commercial bank must collect account payee cheques only for the payee constituent, as the bank shall not collect such cheques for any person other than the payee constituent.

According to [S2], the commercial bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government.

Yes, according to [S1] paragraph 26, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP for CDD in case of new customer onboarding for individual customers and for Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers.

As per the RBI KYC Directions for commercial banks, the bank must ensure that KYC documents are as per current CDD standards; if the documents available are not as per current standards or their validity has expired at periodic updation, it must undertake the KYC process equivalent to onboarding a new customer. Additionally, the bank must verify the customer’s PAN details from the database of the issuing authority at the time of periodic KYC updation. [S1]

According to [S1] para 31, a commercial bank must obtain any two of the listed documents as proof of business/activity for a sole proprietary firm. [S3] para 32 clarifies that if two documents cannot be furnished, the bank may accept only one at its discretion, though the standard requirement remains two.

As stated in [S1], when a commercial bank opens a savings bank account for an SHG, it shall not require CDD of all the members; the CDD of all the office bearers suffices. The bank may undertake CDD of all members at the time of credit linking.
Under the RBI KYC Directions for Commercial Banks (para 20), banks must categorise customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on their assessment and risk perception. [S1]

According to paragraph 83 of the RBI's Responsible Business Conduct Directions, a commercial bank must disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers, enabling them to make an informed judgment about their choice of products [S1].

According to [S1], all aspects concerning renewal of overdue term deposits must be governed by a transparent policy that is non-discretionary and non-discriminatory, and the terms and conditions of renewal, including interest rates, must be notified to the customer at the time of acceptance of the deposit.
Yes, the Directions override and replace existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Responsible Business Conduct as applicable to Commercial Banks, as stated in [S4].

According to [S1] para 58, the bank must make all printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, available in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language.

According to [S1], a commercial bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are put in place and appropriate security measures are taken at each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold or silver collateral. The bank must also ensure that such collateral is handled exclusively within its branches and only by its employees.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 governs the interest rates that commercial banks must offer on deposit accounts and related matters, as [S1] states: "A bank shall be guided by Reserve Bank’s instructions on interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters as prescribed in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025."
As per [S1] para 439, a commercial bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with concentration of exporters to facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters.

[S1] para 363 requires the policy to cover auction procedure specifying the trigger event and timeline for serving an auction notice, the mode of auction, the notice period allowed to borrowers/legal heirs before auction, and the empanelment of auctioneers.

Yes, under [S1] para 87, a bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum BSBD requirements, with or without charges, provided they are offered in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure. The bank cannot require the customer to maintain a minimum balance, and availing such additional facilities is entirely at the customer's option.
[S1] para 192 states that the bank must undertake at least an annual review of accounts where there has been no customer-induced transaction for more than a year.

As stated in [S2], banks should display publicity in bank branches cautioning the public against placing deposits in dubious schemes. [S1] further recommends displaying such messages in bank branches (in the official language of the state), and at ATMs or Business Correspondent Points for wider visibility.

Yes, a commercial bank is held responsible for the conduct of recovery agents it engages. According to [S2], "The bank, as principal, is responsible for the actions of its agents." The bank must therefore ensure its agents strictly adhere to the prescribed instructions while engaged in the recovery of dues.

According to [S1] para 44, the "Enquiry" or "May I Help You" counter should be located near the entry point of the banking hall. It is required at all branches, though very small branches are excluded from this requirement.

According to passage [S1], the prescribed post-shipment interest rate ceases from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account. The text explicitly states: "Although there are instructions that the prescribed post-shipment interest rate will cease from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account..." This directly answers the question regarding when the rate stops accruing for export bills drawn in foreign currency.

According to [S1] para 203, a commercial bank must undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits.

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its outsourced service providers (including subcontractors), which may be performed by the bank's internal or external auditors appointed on its behalf [S1]. These audits shall assess the service provider's performance, risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations, with frequency determined by the nature and extent of risk and impact on the bank [S3]. Additionally, the bank must annually review the service provider's financial and operational condition to assess its ability to meet outsourcing obligations, highlighting any deterioration or breach in performance, confidentiality, security, or business continuity preparedness [S4].

According to [S1], a commercial bank should select a group entity based on objective reasons that are similar to those used for selecting a third-party, and must appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that such an outsourcing arrangement may entail.

According to [S1], the bank bears responsibility for the actions of its service provider, including DSAs/DMAs and recovery agents. Similarly, [S2] states that an NBFC shall be responsible for the actions of its service provider, including DSAs/DMAs and recovery agents, and must retain ultimate control of the outsourced activity.

Based on [S1] paragraph 54, a commercial bank shall ensure that an outsourcing service provider (if not a group company) shall not be owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, approver, or their relatives. However, an exception to this requirement may be made with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight, and monitoring of such arrangements.

According to [S1], sufficient compliance requires clear separation and isolation of the bank's data and its customer-specific data and information, ensuring that only authorized personnel can access data that belongs to them in a multi-tenant environment/architecture.

Yes, a commercial bank remains required to preserve its customers' rights to seek redressal even when outsourcing services to a third-party vendor. According to [S2] (para 94), "Outsourcing arrangements entered into by a bank shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability of the customers to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws." Furthermore, [S3] (para 93) and [S5] (para 51) reinforce that the responsibility for redressal of customers' grievances related to outsourced services rests with the bank and shall not be compromised on account of outsourcing.

Under the RBI's 2025 Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing Directions, the outsourcing agreement must include a clause granting the bank the right to conduct audits on the service provider—whether through its internal or external auditors or appointed agents—and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings made in connection with the services performed for the bank, as specified in paragraph 34(vii) [S2].

Yes, a commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided the arrangement is backed by a Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs or agreements with its group entities are in place, as stated in [S1].

Yes, as stated in [S1], multiple commercial banks availing services from the same third-party IT service provider may adopt a pooled (shared) audit by pooling their audit resources or engaging an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit the provider. However, each RE must ensure that the audit requirements related to their respective contract with the service provider are met effectively.

Paragraph 66 [S1] specifies that banks must consider additional factors such as technology and infrastructural stability, data backup and disaster recovery arrangements, conflict of interest, capability to identify and segregate the bank's data, compliance with regulatory and legal requirements, information/cyber security risk assessment, appropriate controls and contractual arrangements for data protection and bank access, ability to service customers while maintaining confidentiality despite multiple-entity exposure, and the ability to enforce agreements regarding data storage, protection, and confidentiality.

Under paragraph 77 of the RBI Master Directions, a commercial bank must create and maintain an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains. [S2]

A commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the associated costs, time, and resources [S1].

The Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated is responsible for establishing the framework to assess outsourcing risks and materiality. [S1] states that this body "shall be responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements," and [S5] specifies that the Board or a delegated Committee "shall be responsible... for approving a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements."

Yes, the RBI outsourcing requirements apply to subcontracted activities. According to [S3](2), the bank must provide prior approval or consent before the service provider engages any subcontractor, and must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with the Directions in Chapter III. Additionally, [S1](xiii) requires the service provider to be contractually liable for the performance and risk management practices of its subcontractors.

According to paragraph 15 of the RBI Directions, commercial banks shall not outsource core management functions including Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, granting loan sanctions (including retail loans), and managing investment portfolios. [S2]

A bank shall put in place a risk management framework that comprehensively deals with the processes and responsibilities for identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements. [S1] It shall have a management structure to monitor and control its outsourced services, including monitoring performance, uptime, service availability, adherence to SLA requirements, and incident response mechanisms. [S3] Furthermore, outsourcing agreements must contain provisions to address the monitoring and control of outsourced activities. [S4]

Card-issuers must ensure their call centre staff are trained adequately to competently handle and escalate complaints, if necessary. The Grievance Redressal process shall have a provision for automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from the call centre to higher authorities, and a system for acknowledging customers' complaints via complaint/docket numbers even when received over the phone [S1].
According to [S1] para 55, the co-branded card must explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a co-branding arrangement.

According to [S2], card-issuers and their agents must adhere to the extant Fair Practices Code for lenders when recovering dues, meaning they must avoid any practices not compliant with that code. [S1] further requires that collection agents refrain from actions that could damage the card-issuer's integrity and reputation, and must observe strict customer confidentiality.

No, a commercial bank does not need prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India before issuing co-branded credit cards, debit cards, or prepaid cards. Paragraph 54 of the "Commercial Banks - Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct" chapter explicitly states that prior approval is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards and co-branded credit cards subject to conditions stipulated under the chapter. [S1]

According to [S2] para 11(6), if no OTP-based consent is received for activating a credit card, the card-issuer must close the account within seven working days from the date of seeking confirmation from the customer. [S1] para 11 Explanation confirms the same seven-working-day timeframe for closing the account when the customer does not respond to the consent request.

The monetary threshold is one percent of the credit limit or ₹5,000, whichever is lower, as provided in [S1]. This triggers the explicit consent requirement for commercial banks when adjusting refund amounts against the credit limit after the bill has already been paid.
The card-issuer must explicitly bring to the notice of the customer that such information is being provided in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. [S1]

According to [S1], all communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number, and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact. This ensures cardholders have direct access to a senior officer for resolution of their concerns.

According to [S2], a commercial bank may report a credit card account as ‘past due’ to credit information companies or levy late-payment charges only when the account remains past due for more than three days. The number of days past due is computed from the payment due date mentioned in the credit card statement.

No, a commercial bank cannot levy charges on a credit or debit card that were not disclosed to the cardholder at the time of issuance. [S1] states that card-issuers shall not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholders at the time of issue of the card and without getting their explicit consent. This prohibition does not apply to charges like service taxes subsequently levied by the Government or other statutory authorities.
Yes, a commercial bank may issue a business credit card to an individual for business-related spending, as [S1] explicitly permits card-issuers to do so for business expenses.

A commercial bank's credit card issuance and conduct policy must be well-documented, approved by its Board or a delegated Committee, and available on the bank's website, as required by [S1] para 8. Additionally, the policy must cover interest rate ceilings and other charges, procedures for reporting default to a Credit Information Company, co-branding arrangements, standard operating procedures for discretionary card blocking/deactivation/suspension, time periods for completing formalities after blocking a lost card, and a grievance redressal and compensation framework, as detailed in [S3] para 9.
Card-issuers shall ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders." [S1]

According to [S4] para 91, card-issuers shall provide the cardholder with a term-sheet containing the MITC. This document must include details on fees and charges, drawal limits, billing procedures, and default and circumstances.

You may disclose customer information to DSAs, DMAs, and recovery agents only to the extent necessary for them to discharge their duties. Personal information provided by the cardholder but not required for recovery purposes shall not be released, as stated in [S1].

According to [S1] para 42, a commercial bank has the freedom to determine interest on deposits accepted or renewed under the RFC Account Scheme, in accordance with a comprehensive policy on interest rates on deposits duly approved by the Board of Directors or any Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated.

According to [S1] para 11(1), if a customer withdraws a domestic term deposit before maturity, the bank must pay interest at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank, not at the contracted rate. [S1] para 11(2) adds that no interest is paid if the withdrawal occurs before the minimum period specified in para 10(1).
According to [S1], the minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year and for NRO term deposits is seven days.

As stated in [S1], a commercial bank must be authorised under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time in order to accept rupee deposits from non-residents under NRE and NRO accounts.

Yes, a commercial bank can pay additional interest on deposits held by its staff members and their exclusive associations. Paragraph 12 of the RBI guidelines specifies that the maximum additional rate permitted is one per cent per annum over and above the scheduled interest rate, as stated in [S1].

According to [S1], paragraph 30, a commercial bank must treat a deceased depositor's NRE term deposit as a domestic rupee term deposit at maturity if the claimant(s) are residents. In such cases, the deposit on maturity is treated as a domestic rupee term deposit, and interest for the subsequent period is paid at the rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity.

According to [S2], paragraph 20, the interest rate on matured deposits standing in the name of a deceased individual depositor shall be "as per comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits and subject to the conditions laid down in paragraph 7 of these Directions." The passages do not specify a fixed numerical rate but reference the applicable policy framework and conditions.

According to [S1] paragraph 41(1), if the components of penalty are not clearly brought to the notice of the depositors at the time of acceptance of the deposits, then the exchange loss arising out of premature withdrawal shall be borne by the bank.

According to [S1] para 35(1), if the renewal occurs within 14 days of maturity, the interest rate payable is whichever is lower between the rate prevailing on the date of maturity and the rate on the date the depositor seeks renewal.

According to [S1], paragraph 46 states that "Notwithstanding such repeal, any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof." Therefore, yes, any action taken by a commercial bank under the previous Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions before they were repealed will still be governed by those old rules.

A commercial bank is prohibited from charging a penalty for premature withdrawal of a domestic term deposit in the event of the depositor's death, even if the deposit is within a lock-in-period [S1]. Additionally, no penalty shall be levied when splitting the amount of a term deposit at the request of claimants of deceased depositors or joint account holders, provided the period and aggregate amount of the deposit do not undergo any change [S2]. Furthermore, no penalty shall be levied for premature withdrawal consequent to the transfer of business to another bank, for depositors of the branch mentioned in paragraph 7(9) [S4].

Yes, according to [S1] para 14, a bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates as admissible to senior citizens, over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of their being retired members of the bank’s staff. This explicitly permits the extra rate on top of the staff retirement benefit.

As stated in paragraph 21 of the RBI Directions [S1], the minimum credit balance in a farmer's composite cash credit account is measured for interest purposes during the period from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month.

As per [S4] para 7(1), a commercial bank's Board-approved deposit policy must cover interest rates on deposits, penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits (including partial premature withdrawal), penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits, and penalties for premature withdrawal of FCNR(B) term deposits. [S2] para 22 additionally requires a comprehensive policy on penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits, including partial premature withdrawal, approved by the Board or a delegated committee.

As stated in [S3], banks may use foreign currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB dated December 17, 2018, as well as foreign currency funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market, to extend PCFC, subject to adherence to the Aggregate Gap Limit (AGL).

According to [S1], a bank's exposure through PCEs to bonds issued by a single NBFC or HFC is restricted to one per cent of the capital funds of the RE, within the extant single/group borrower exposure limits. This is the specific maximum exposure cap for such PCE arrangements.

Under the RBI’s Commercial Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, all corporates and other constituent borrowers having turnover above the threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors must disclose the ‘aging schedule’ of their overdue payables in their periodical returns submitted to banks. [S1]

According to passage [S1], paragraph 247, the bank must grant export credit to exporters of good track record until the proceeds of the cheque or draft received from abroad are realized, provided it is satisfied that the credit is against an export order, complies with trade practices for the goods in question, and is an approved method of realizing export proceeds under extant rules.

According to [S1], paragraph 118, when a commercial bank introduces any kind of product, it must take into account the customer's suitability and appropriateness, and ensure that borrowers/customers are fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products. This requirement applies to new lending products as part of the bank's product introduction process.

According to [S1](4), a commercial bank must verify the genuineness of the documents to the title of the property mortgaged with the bank at the time of acceptance, and not defer this verification until the initiation of recovery proceedings. This ensures that title documents are validated before funds are released for a real estate loan.

According to [S1] para 119(1) and (3), when a commercial bank finances a specific housing or development project, the builder/developer/company must disclose the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged in the pamphlets/brochures, and indicate that they will provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC)/permission of the mortgagee bank for sale of flats/property if required.

Yes. According to [S1] para 225, "As banks can extend financial assistance to equipment leasing companies, they shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with such companies as well as other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing." Similarly, [S2] para 42(2) states: "A bank shall not enter into leasing agreement with another equipment leasing company and other non-banking finance company engaged in equipment leasing."

According to [S1], paragraph 364 states that bills rediscounted 'with recourse' in the domestic market shall not be reckoned as export credit by the rediscounting bank, as only the first bank discounting the bills has recourse to the exporter.

As per [S2], a commercial bank must determine the value of gold or silver collateral by taking the lower of either the average closing price over the preceding 30 days or the closing price on the preceding day, for the specific purity (caratage), as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd. (IBJA) or a commodity exchange regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).

[S5] para 62 states that all collateral-free loans provided to low-income households (i.e., households with annual income up to ₹3,00,000), irrespective of end use and mode of application/disbursal (physical or digital channels), are considered microfinance loans. The explanation further specifies that such loans must not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by hypothecation of any security to maintain their collateral-free nature.

Under [S1] para 85, a commercial bank must capture and maintain project-specific data in electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis. The project finance database must include, at a minimum, the Debtor Profile, Original Project Profile, and Change in DCCO, with the specified parameters for each. These requirements ensure ongoing tracking of project details such as sponsor information, financial closure dates, debt/equity ratios, and DCCO changes.

According to [S1] para 96, commercial banks shall not grant finance for the construction of buildings meant purely for Government/Semi-Government offices, including Municipal offices. The passage explicitly prohibits such financing, though an exception exists for loans that will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD.

According to [S1], a commercial bank may accept DLG only in one or more of the following forms: (1) Cash deposited with the bank, (2) a Fixed Deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, or (3) a Bank Guarantee in favour of the bank.

According to [S1] para 4, an Internet Banking Channel is defined as a digital banking channel operated over the internet using web browser‑based applications but excluding mobile applications, whereas a Mobile Banking Channel is defined as one operated using mobile applications, unstructured supplementary service data (USSD), and short message service (SMS).

Yes, under para 11 of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, the Reserve Bank may exempt any regulated entity, including commercial banks, from all or any provisions of the Directions either generally or for a specified period to avoid hardship or for other just and sufficient reasons, subject to such conditions as the Reserve Bank may impose. [S1]

As stated in [S1] para 9, point 1, commercial banks conducting digital banking operations must comply with the Information Technology Act, 2000, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, FEMA 1999, KYC/AML/CFT directions, and other legal requirements, and the jurisdiction of legal settlement is within India.

According to [S1], a commercial bank must obtain prior approval from the Reserve Bank before launching a transactional banking facility, fulfilling eligibility criteria such as CBS implementation, regulatory CRAR compliance, minimum paid-up capital/Net worth, and adequate financial/technical capabilities. The bank is required to apply to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India, through the PRAVAAH portal, along with the approval of the appropriate authority and other necessary supporting documents.

According to [S1] para 10.1, banks must obtain explicit consent from customers for registering or de-registering for digital banking services, with the consent duly recorded. The same provision requires that customers be clearly informed that SMS/email alerts will be sent to their registered mobile number/email for all account operations.

According to [S1] para 14 and [S4] para 79, the RBI's interpretation of any provision of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions is final and binding on all concerned entities. Therefore, as a compliance officer, you can rely on the RBI's interpretation when a provision is ambiguous, as it carries authoritative and binding weight.

As stated in [S1] para 8(1), banks offering digital banking services must follow the Guidelines on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services as specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025. [S2] para 54 further specifies that any outsourced model for digital banking segments, including DBUs, must specifically comply with the relevant regulatory guidelines on outsourcing contained in the 2025 Directions.

According to [S1] para 6.1, a bank must have implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled its public-facing IT infrastructure to handle Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) traffic to be eligible for offering a view-only banking facility. [S1] para 6.2 further requires such banks to submit a Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) report via the PRAVAAH portal within thirty days of launch, subject to scrutiny by supervisors.

Under [S1] para 5, banks shall put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels, keeping in account all statutory and regulatory requirements, including the management of liquidity and operational risks in the digital banking scenario.

According to [S1] paragraph 20(1), the bank should consider lodging a formal complaint against the statutory auditors of the borrowers with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) / Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) to examine and fix their accountability. Furthermore, per [S1] paragraph 20(2), pending disciplinary action, the complaint must be forwarded to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and Indian Banks' Association (IBA), after satisfying itself of the auditors' involvement and providing them an opportunity to be heard.

According to [S1], the responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank. Furthermore, [S1] specifies that a bank must ensure the accuracy of the particulars of directors and, wherever possible, cross-check with the database maintained by the Registrar of Companies when furnishing information to credit information companies.

According to [S1], paragraph 7(3)(2), the bar on additional credit facility to a wilful defaulter or any associated entity shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of the wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders. This one-year restriction applies specifically to the prohibition on granting additional credit facilities.

According to [S2] paragraph 15(1), the name of a borrower or guarantor classified as a wilful defaulter must be removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters after the implementation of the resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code or the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025.

A commercial bank must put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identification of wilful defaulters so that the penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated. [S1]

According to [S1] paragraph 12(1), a commercial bank must submit information on wilful defaulters to credit information companies at monthly intervals. The report must include, in Annex II, a list of wilful defaulters (LWD) for suit-filed accounts and a separate LWD for non-suit-filed accounts.

As per [S1] para 21, a commercial bank must forward the details of third parties that played a vital role in credit sanction/disbursement and were negligent in a wilful default case to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, regardless of membership status; IBA then prepares caution lists circulated to all regulated RBI entities. Before such reporting, the bank must satisfy itself of the third party's involvement and provide them an opportunity to be heard, following due process suitably recorded.

According to [S1], paragraph 10(2), "When a default happens in making payment / repayment by the principal debtor, a bank shall be able to proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor." This means the bank may pursue the guarantor directly upon the borrower's default, without first exhausting remedies against the borrower.

Yes, the Reserve Bank of India may issue necessary clarifications on how to apply the Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions, as stated in [S1]: "the Reserve Bank may, if it considers necessary, issue necessary clarifications in respect of any matter covered herein." Furthermore, the interpretation of any provision given by the Reserve Bank "shall be final and binding."

Yes, a commercial bank must report to credit information companies the details of guarantors who fail to honour commitments when invoked, classifying them as large defaulters or wilful defaulters as the case may be, as per [S1]. Such guarantors are classified as wilful defaulters if the outstanding amount is ₹25 lakh and above, or as may be notified by RBI from time to time, per [S3], and must follow the classification mechanism outlined in [S4] if they refuse to comply with the bank's demand.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025 apply to commercial banks, defined as all banking companies, corresponding new banks, and State Bank of India under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, while explicitly excluding Small Finance Banks, Local Area Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks [S4].

According to [S1], a bank must require its internal auditors to specifically look into adherence to instructions for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter. This requirement is stated in paragraph 9(1) of the Commercial Banks guidelines on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters.

According to [S2](1), a commercial bank can remove a wilful defaulter's name from the List of Wilful Defaulters only after the borrower has fully paid the compromise amount. [S2](2) adds that until full payment is made, the name shall not be removed from the LWD even if the outstanding amount falls below the ₹25 lakh threshold. Thus, full settlement of the compromise amount is the mandatory condition for removal.

According to [S5], the RBI's Commercial Banks (Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025 apply "in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force." This means the directions supplement existing legal and regulatory frameworks rather than replacing them, so as a compliance officer, you must ensure adherence to both the new directions and all currently enforceable laws.

According to paragraph 14 of the RBI Governance Directions, quarterly statements on change of directors must reach the relevant RBI Regional Office within 15 days of the close of each respective quarter. [S3]

According to [S1], an NBFC-P2P shall comply with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices dated November 07, 2023 (as amended from time to time).

As stated in [S4], the Board of Directors must provide for periodical review of the compliance of the Fair Practices Code and the functioning of the grievance redressal mechanism at various levels of management, with a consolidated report submitted to the Board at regular intervals.

At least two escrow accounts must be maintained: a Lenders’ escrow Account for funds received from lenders pending disbursal, and a Borrowers’ escrow Account for collections from borrowers. Funds from the Lenders’ escrow account shall not be used for loan repayment, and funds from the Borrowers’ escrow account shall not be used for loan disbursement, with all transfers conducted exclusively through bank accounts [S1].

According to paragraph 67 of the RBI Directions, prior written permission is required for any allotment of shares that takes the aggregate holding of an individual or group to 26 per cent or more of the paid-up capital of the NBFC-P2P. [S1]
As stated in [S1], an NBFC-P2P must conduct an information system audit of its internal systems and processes at least once in two years by CISA certified external auditors.

Yes, an NBFC-P2P is allowed to follow the RBI's Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience. Paragraph 60 of the Non-Banking Financial Companies - Peer to Peer Lending Platform guidelines explicitly states: "An NBFC-P2P may make use of the ‘ Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience’, as amended from time to time." Paragraph 4 of the NBFC-P2P Directions explicitly states that the listed RBI directions "shall be applicable to an NBFC-P2P where not contradictory to the contents of these Directions" ([S1] para 4). This is further reinforced by specific compliance requirements in [S2] para 31, [S3] para 71, [S4] para 73, and [S5] para 41, which all reference those same RBI directions alongside the P2P platform rules.

Yes, the RBI may impose additional conditions beyond the standard eligibility requirements for registering an NBFC-P2P platform. [S2] paragraph 15(9) explicitly authorizes the Reserve Bank to specify "any other condition... necessary to ensure that the commencement of or carrying on the business in India shall not be prejudicial to the public interest." This is further supported by [S3] paragraph 16, which grants in-principle approval "subject to such conditions which it may consider fit to impose," and [S5] paragraph 19, which states that a Certificate of Registration is granted "subject to conditions as deemed fit by the Reserve Bank."

According to [S1] para 39, an NBFC-P2P must comply with the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 for reporting and updating credit information relating to borrower transactions on the platform. Furthermore, the NBFC-P2P is required to include necessary consents in agreements with participants for providing such credit information.

The Leverage Ratio for an NBFC-P2P is calculated as Total Outside Liabilities divided by Owned Funds, as defined in [S4]. [S1] further clarifies that customers’ funds lent or borrowed using the platform are not reckoned as outside liability in this calculation.

No, the platform cannot hold your lent funds on its own balance sheet. According to [S1](6), an NBFC-P2P shall not hold on its own balance sheet the funds received from lenders for lending. This is further reinforced in [S4], which states that customers' funds lent via the platform cannot be utilised by the platform.

The passages indicate that the RBI's 2025 P2P Lending Platform Directions do not replace other laws, rules, regulations, or directions. [S1] states that the provisions of multiple other RBI directions "shall be applicable to an NBFC-P2P, where not contradictory to the contents of these Directions," meaning the 2025 P2P Directions coexist with other regulatory frameworks subject to a non-contradiction condition. Therefore, the 2025 Directions operate alongside, not as a replacement for, other applicable RBI directions and regulations.

An NBFC-P2P must communicate changes of address, directors, and auditors to the Reserve Bank, as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of the Miscellaneous Directions, 2025 [S1]. Additionally, any change in directors or key management personnel must be reported within 15 days, accompanied by a certificate from the Managing Director/CEO confirming fit and proper criteria were followed, and an annual statement of directors certified by auditors must be submitted [S4].

An NBFC-P2P must establish a Fair Practices Code with the approval of its Board and publish it on its website for stakeholders ([S1]). The Fair Practices Code is also one of the Board-approved policies the NBFC-P2P must put in place to ensure sound processes and systems ([S4]).
Paragraph 45 states that an NBFC-AA shall form a Nomination Committee consisting of not less than three members of its Board of Directors. [S1]

As an NBFC-AA, you must follow the disclosure requirements specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025, as stated in [S5]. However, specific exemptions apply: provisions contained in paragraphs 13 to 15 and paragraph 20 of those Directions are excluded for NBFC-AA, as noted in [S3]. Additionally, [S2] allows omitting inapplicable line items or disclosures if there is no exposure or transaction in the current and previous year.

According to [S1], every NBFC-AA shall communicate change of address, directors, auditors, etc., as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025.

The Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 apply to every non-banking financial company undertaking the business of Account Aggregator as defined herein. [S1]

Paragraph 28 explicitly states that such information "shall not be used or disclosed by an NBFC-AA or the Financial Information User except as may be specified in the consent artefact." [S1]

According to [S1] para 27, the NBFC-AA must verify the identity of the Financial Information User before transferring the information. If verified, it must securely transfer the customer’s information to the intended recipient in accordance with the terms of the consent artefact.

Under [S1], an NBFC-AA must have a Board approved policy for pricing of services, which must be transparent and available in the public domain. [S4] similarly requires the Board to approve policies on Pricing of Services as part of its sound processes and systems.

NBFC-AA is always placed in the Base Layer under the Scale Based Regulation framework. [S1] states: "NBFC-AA shall always remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure specified in Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025." [S2] confirms in paragraph 15(1): "NBFC-AA ... will always remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure."

As stated in [S5] paragraph 34, it is the responsibility of the NBFC-AA to ensure its IT systems have all features necessary to carry out its functions strictly in conformity with the Directions as updated from time to time. Furthermore, [S1] paragraph 30(3) requires the technology to be scalable to cover any other financial information or Financial Information Provider as may be specified by the Reserve Bank in future.

The standardized consent artefact must contain the customer's identity and optional contact information, the nature of the financial information requested, the purpose of collecting such information, the identity of recipients if any, a URL or other address for usage notifications, the consent creation and expiry dates along with the NBFC-AA's identity and signature, and any other attribute prescribed by the Reserve Bank [S1].

A Non-Banking Financial Company classified as a Credit Institution covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme must comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme, as explicitly stated in [S1]. This compliance obligation is reiterated for NBFCs under the 2021 Integrated Ombudsman Scheme in [S2] and [S4]. The passages uniformly establish that coverage of the scheme mandates adherence to its prescribed directions.
According to [S2], the Sub-Group of TWG shall meet at least on a half yearly basis to discuss credit information reporting issues and seek potential resolutions.

According to paragraph 24 of the RBI's Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025, the Technical Working Group (TWG) comprises representatives from Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), All India Notified Financial Institutions (AIFIs), Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), the India Banks’ Association (IBA), the Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN), Sa-Dhan, and Credit Information Companies (CICs). As per [S2] paragraph 63, the ARC must obtain and verify the customer's PAN or equivalent e-document while undertaking transactions, as required under Income Tax Rule 114B. If the customer does not have a PAN, Form 60 must be obtained instead.

According to [S1], paragraph (6), if an existing KYC-compliant customer of an ARC desires to open another account or avail of any other product or service from the same ARC, there shall be no need for a fresh CDD exercise as far as identification of the customer is concerned.

According to [S1], if a non-profit organisation customer is not registered on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog, the Asset Reconstruction Company shall register the details on the DARPAN Portal. The ARC must also maintain such registration records for a period of five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later.

An Asset Reconstruction Company must apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of money laundering and terrorist financing risks, with Board-approved policies, controls, and a Customer Due Diligence (CDD) programme proportionate to identified risks and business size [S1]. [S3] further requires the ARC to undertake ML/TF risk assessments prior to launching new products or technologies and to manage risks through appropriate Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) measures and transaction monitoring. Additionally, [S4] permits the ARC to adopt best international practices, including FATF standards, for more effective risk management.

As stated in [S1], the Asset Reconstruction Company must review its money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually. The periodicity of the exercise is determined by the Board or a committee of the Board to which the power has been delegated.
An NBFC must undertake diligence measures and meticulous monitoring to identify accounts operated as money mules and report suspicious transactions to FIU-IND. [S1]

An NBFC can transfer a customer's account to another branch of the same NBFC without carrying out fresh KYC checks if it has already completed the full KYC verification for the concerned account and the same is not due for periodic updation. [S1]

According to [S1], paragraph 51, a delay of each day in not reporting a transaction or delay of each day in rectifying a mis-represented transaction beyond the time limit specified in the Rule shall constitute as a separate violation for the NBFC.

Yes, [S1] paragraph 4 states that the RBI’s KYC/AML directions apply to branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of All India Financial Institutions located abroad, to the extent they are not contradictory to local laws in the host country. The passage further specifies that if local laws prohibit implementation, the AIFI must notify the RBI, and where there is a variance in standards, the more stringent regulation applies.

According to [S1] para 21(2), an All India Financial Institution must identify a customer who is not an account holder when carrying out any international money transfer operations for that person. This is explicitly listed as a case where the AIFI shall undertake identification of customers.

As stated in [S1] paragraph 36, a small finance bank must obtain the trust's registration certificate and the trust's PAN or Form No. 60 as the required registration and tax-identification documents before opening an account.

According to [S1], the four key elements of an All India Financial Institution's KYC policy are: (i) Customer Acceptance Policy, (ii) Risk Management, (iii) Customer Identification Procedures (CIP), and (iv) Monitoring of Transactions.

According to [S1] para 62(2), an All India Financial Institution must upload the customer’s KYC records to the Central KYC Records Registry within 10 days of commencement of an account-based relationship with the customer.

According to [S2], a rural co-operative bank may utilize the at-par cheque facility only for its own use, for its KYC-compliant account-holders (with transactions of ₹50,000 or more strictly by debit to accounts), and for walk-in customers against cash for less than ₹50,000 per individual. The bank must also maintain records of cheque issuance covering applicant and beneficiary details, ensure sufficient balances or drawing arrangements with the commercial bank, and cross all ‘at par’ cheques as ‘account payee’ irrespective of amount.

According to [S1], an Urban Co-operative Bank must apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks, and shall have Board-approved policies, controls and procedures in this regard.

According to [S1], for an urban co-operative bank using a commercial bank’s at-par cheque facility for KYC-compliant account holders, all transactions of ₹50,000 or more must be strictly debited to the customers’ accounts.

A Regional Rural Bank must apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks, having regard to ML/TF risks and the size of business, and shall have Board-approved policies, controls, and procedures in this regard, as stated in [S2]. The bank shall also implement a CDD programme and monitor the implementation of controls, enhancing them if necessary, per [S2].

According to [S1] para 25(3), the aggregate balance of all deposit accounts for a customer opened via Aadhaar OTP-based e-KYC must not exceed Rupees One Lakh. If this cap is breached, the bank shall cease the account’s operation until it completes the CDD procedure as mentioned in paragraph 25(5).

According to [S3], a Payments Bank must ensure that the maintenance of records under rule 3 of the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and the furnishing of information to the Director, FIU-IND, remain confidential. However, this confidentiality requirement does not inhibit sharing of information under paragraph 8 of the Directions regarding any analysis of transactions and activities that appear unusual, provided the bank has conducted such analysis.

[S1] specifies that "a delay of each day in not reporting a transaction or delay of each day in rectifying a mis-represented transaction beyond the time limit as specified in the Rule shall constitute as a separate violation." This means each individual day of delay is counted as a distinct violation.

According to [S1], a Payments Bank shall not require CDD of all the members of an SHG while opening the savings bank account of the SHG; the CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice. Therefore, a Payments Bank does not need to conduct Customer Due Diligence on every member of an SHG when opening a savings account for the group.
According to [S1] para 80(1), the bank must put in place an adequate screening mechanism, including a Know Your Employee/Staff policy, as an integral part of its personnel recruitment/hiring process.
